title: Beyond Binary Rewards: Training LMs to Reason About Their Uncertainty
one_liner: Train reasoning models with rewards that chase both correct answers AND confident guesses, so they stop hallucinating.
lead: Language models trained with standard reinforcement learning learn to reason better and get more questions right, because the reward signal nudges the model's outputs in whichever direction lowers error. But they develop a blind spot: they become overconfident, spitting out wrong answers without hesitation, because the reward only scored whether the answer matched the truth—it said nothing about how sure to be. This paper shows how to fix that by changing the reward signal itself. Instead of just rewarding right answers, reward right answers that come with appropriate confidence, measured by a standard confidence score (called a Brier score). Models trained this way stay accurate while becoming genuinely calibrated—they learn to say 'I'm not sure' when they should, because the Brier score creates a mathematical penalty that forces confidence numbers to track actual correctness or the model gets a lower reward.

problem.h2: Why do reasoning models get overconfident?
paras: When you train a model with reinforcement learning using simple rewards ('right or wrong, 1 or 0'), the model learns to maximize that score. It learns to say the right answer. But the reward signal says nothing about how confident to be. A model trained this way can answer a hard question correctly one day and confidently hallucinate (make up a plausible-sounding but false answer) the next day, because there's no penalty for guessing when you're unsure.

The naive fix would be: add a confidence classifier after the model finishes, a separate post-hoc tuner that tries to guess how confident the model should sound. But that's like a student who memorizes answers perfectly then tries to figure out which answers to fake confidence about. The confidence is bolted on, disconnected from the real reasoning.

callout.html: RL training for reasoning optimizes only correctness, ignoring confidence, so models become overconfident and hallucinate.

steps.text: Standard chain of thought, just like before.
A final answer AND a confidence number from 0 to 1.
Check if the answer was right: 1 if yes, 0 if no.
Measure the squared gap (confidence minus correctness). High confidence on a wrong answer is penalized hard.

RL update pushes the model to improve both: get answers right AND match confidence to correctness, because the reward is a single number that penalizes both wrongness and overconfidence equally, so the model must find the path through its reasoning that maximizes the combined score.

paras: The paper changes the reward function from a single binary score to a combined score that rewards both correctness and calibration. The model still generates reasoning chains, outputs, and confidence estimates—the architecture doesn't change. Only what we measure and reward changes.

hidden.name: calibration error (squared gap between confidence and correctness)
paras: Calibration is a simple idea: if the model says it's 70 percent confident, it should be right about 70 percent of the time on those statements. If it says 99 percent confident but is only right 50 percent of the time, it's badly calibrated (overconfident). The Brier score measures this by taking the difference between stated confidence and actual correctness, squaring it, and averaging over many examples.

The paper computes this Brier score during training and includes it in the reward. A model that says it's 90 percent sure about a wrong answer gets heavily penalized. One that says 55 percent sure about an answer it gets right also gets penalized, but much less. Over many training steps, the model learns to output confidence numbers that actually match reality.

heat.caption: Darker=higher reward. Boxes mark best (high-conf-correct and low-conf-wrong) and worst (high-conf-wrong) scenarios for training.

reads.html: Calibration is how often what the model says about its own certainty turns out to be true. A calibrated model never says I am sure and then fails.

The Brier score, a proper scoring rule, penalizes distance between predicted confidence and observed binary outcome. It is computed as the average of the squared gap between confidence and correctness.

mechanism.h2: Why mixing correctness and calibration works
paras: A proper scoring rule like Brier has a mathematical property: if a model learns to minimize it, the model must output confidences that match reality. There is no shortcut—the model cannot cheat by always guessing 0.5 or always saying 99 percent. The only way to lower the Brier score is to output confidence numbers that honestly reflect how often the model is correct.

During training, the RL algorithm (GRPO, a method that adjusts the model's outputs to maximize reward) uses this combined reward to nudge the model. When the model gets an answer right and outputs high confidence, the training adjustment says 'good, do more of this.' When it gets an answer wrong and outputs high confidence, the adjustment says 'bad, fix this—either get it right or admit uncertainty.' Over thousands of training steps, the model learns to route its confidence through the same reasoning process that produced the answer. The reasoning and the confidence become coupled, not bolted on.

stages.s: Measure squared gap between confidence and correctness
Reward equals rightness minus penalty for mismatch
Training steers model: improve answers and align confidence, because adjustments that increase the combined reward become more likely in future runs

math.words: Reward equals 1 if the answer is correct else 0, minus a penalty strength times the Brier score (squared gap between stated confidence and actual correctness)
symbols: 1 if the answer is correct, 0 if wrong
penalty strength: how much to punish miscalibration

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Scenario A: Model answers correctly and says 90% confident. Correctness = 1, confidence = 0.9. Gap = (0.9 - 1)^2 = 0.01. With lambda = 1, reward = 1 - 1*0.01 = 0.99.
Scenario B: Model answers incorrectly but says 80% confident. Correctness = 0, confidence = 0.8. Gap = (0.8 - 0)^2 = 0.64. With lambda = 1, reward = 0 - 1*0.64 = -0.64.
Scenario C: Model answers correctly but says 20% confident. Correctness = 1, confidence = 0.2. Gap = (0.2 - 1)^2 = 0.64. With lambda = 1, reward = 1 - 1*0.64 = 0.36.
The key: A and C both sacrifice points for miscalibration, but A (right + high confidence) loses less than B (wrong + high confidence). The model learns the optimal tradeoff: get it right AND say so.

math.note: The formula enforces an honest trade-off: accuracy alone gives a higher reward than either high confidence without correctness or low confidence with correctness. Over training, the model learns that the safest path is to align confidence with its actual reasoning quality.

charts.title: Ordinary RL training (binary reward only)
charts.note: Model improves accuracy but becomes overconfident, because the model learned that saying 'I'm sure' is free—there is no cost to high confidence even when the model is guessing. Calibration gets worse because confidence is never penalized.

charts.title: RLCR (binary + Brier score)
charts.note: Accuracy stays strong because correctness is still rewarded, and calibration improves dramatically, because the Brier penalty makes high confidence on wrong answers costly—the model now learns that saying 'I'm unsure' on hard questions lowers the penalty more than wrongly claiming certainty. The model's confidence now aligns with reality even on new domains because the learned link between reasoning quality and stated uncertainty generalizes.

items.b: If lambda is too high, model learns to be uncertain.
items.html: Calibration improves but accuracy drops—the model trades correctness for the safety of low confidence, because if the penalty for overconfidence (lambda) exceeds the benefit of correctness, the model finds it mathematically easier to just say 'I'm 10 percent sure' on everything than to risk the penalty of being wrong and confident. Tuning lambda balances the two.

items.b: If the training data is mislabeled, confidence becomes meaningless.
items.html: The model learns to match its confidence to corrupted labels. In that regime, Brier score rewards false confidence on wrong answers.

items.b: Confidence on very different data may still be miscalibrated.
items.html: If test questions are very different from training, the model's learned confidence estimates may not hold up. The paper shows out-of-domain improvement, but extreme shifts remain a risk.

Tune lambda on a validation set, clean your labels, and test on data similar enough to training that reasoning skills transfer. Confidence will track accuracy in the domain where the model was trained.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small reasoning model trained on a dataset like GSM8K or HotpotQA. Split your data into train and test. Train one copy with ordinary binary-reward RL and another with RLCR (binary plus Brier). For each model, compute: (1) accuracy (fraction of questions answered correctly), (2) average confidence on correct vs incorrect answers, and (3) Brier score (mean squared gap across all test examples). The visualization should show: (a) a chart of accuracy for both models (they stay close), (b) a chart of calibration on test (RLCR's confidence and correctness track each other; ordinary RL's don't), and (c) a few example questions with side-by-side confidences from each model, highlighting cases where RLCR says low confidence on a hard question while ordinary RL confidently hallucinated.
demo.metric_eq: calibration error = average over all examples of (stated confidence - actual correctness)^2
demo.closing: The demo must make impossible to miss: models trained with Brier rewards output lower confidence on questions they get wrong, even if those questions look similar to ones they got right.
